title: Themes, not maps: mined question groups, author-published presentation (including basemap), and a readable solution write-up
problem: TR-VIS-0008 gave the consumer a catalogue of decision maps and their tests, and it works. But the product framing is wrong in two ways. First, a reader does not arrive wanting 'maps'; they arrive with a question, and the questions repeat across conversations. The interesting unit is therefore a THEME — a recurring question group mined from conversation history — and a map is one published answer to it. Second, the answers are increasingly authored outside this chatbot: hackathon and data-jam participants write their own mining scripts and publish analyses through the totalrecall publisher. When their work is rendered here it currently loses its identity — the consumer imposes its own basemap and its own layout, so a published solution looks like a generic figure rather than the author's piece of work. The catalogue also carries no prose: `decision`, `product` and `validation.method` are contract fields, not an explanation a reader can follow, so the consumer has nothing honest to show as 'here is the solution'. Finally, the site-selection landing wants to place each pack as a light on a dark field, and no endpoint reports where a pack actually is.
evidence: The consumer shipped TR-VIS-0008 in full (see dss/integration/responses/TR-VIS-0008/): catalogue-driven centre, validation beside every map, fail-closed selection styling, colour-independent marks for fitting/withheld/selected. Nothing in this request replaces that; the validation treatment is exactly what should travel with a published solution.

decision_maps.json already carries `questions` per recipe — three per Valparai recipe, phrased the way a person would ask them ('Where should we restart roadkill monitoring?'). That field is the seed of a theme, but nothing says how often the question was actually asked, or which conversations it was mined from.

The consumer renders maps through two renderers (an SVG figure map inline, Leaflet in the panel) and currently owns basemap choice: a hardcoded imagery/streets pair plus a per-reader localStorage preference. An author who published a dark carto basemap, a terrain basemap, or no basemap at all has no way to say so.

`recipe.limitations`, `validation.claim_if_passed/claim_if_failed` and `product.*` are single sentences aimed at the contract, and the consumer already renders them. What is missing is the author's own explanation of what they did and what it means — the thing a data-jam entry would be judged on.

GET /v1/capabilities returns site_id, label, pack_digest, synthetic and the capability list. It reports no bounds, centroid or extent, so the consumer cannot place a pack on a map without querying site-orientation per pack and reading geometry out of an envelope built for a different purpose.
requested_outcome: GET /v1/themes — the mined question groups this pack publishes, as a leaderboard. Each theme: stable `theme_id`, human `title` phrased as the question people actually ask, the `questions` variants it absorbs, a `mined` block (how many conversations it was seen in, first/last seen, and the mining run or script identity so the count can be audited), a `status`, and the `solutions` that answer it. Themes with no solution yet are legitimate and must be returnable — an unanswered recurring question is a finding.

A theme's `solutions[]` entries carry: `solution_id`, `title`, `author` (name and optional affiliation/handle — a data jam has authors and they should be credited), `published_at`, the `capability_id` + `arguments` that produce the result (today: validated-decision-map + recipe_id), and a `writeup`. The write-up is the author's own explanation in plain prose or restricted markdown (headings, paragraphs, lists, emphasis, links — no raw HTML, no scripts), long enough to be read as an answer rather than a caption.

A `presentation` block, per solution and/or per visual, that lets the author's published styling survive the consumer's rendering. At minimum: `basemap` — one of a producer-declared set (or a declared tile template with attribution and max zoom), plus `theme` ('dark' | 'light') so the surrounding chrome can match; optional `initial_view` (bounds or centre+zoom); optional per-layer style intent already carried by style_hint. The consumer will honour the declared basemap for that solution instead of its own default, keep the attribution the producer supplies, and fall back to its default only when nothing is declared.

If a declared basemap requires an external tile host, declare it as an id the consumer proxies — the consumer must not let the browser call a third-party host directly (same-origin CSP and the existing tile proxy are non-negotiable). A producer-declared id the consumer does not recognise must degrade to the consumer default rather than fail the render.
GET /v1/themes/{theme_id} — the theme with its full solution list and write-ups, for the reading view.

Extend GET /v1/capabilities with the pack's geography: `bounds` (west, south, east, north) and/or `centroid` (lon, lat), plus an optional `weight` the pack considers representative of its size (or let the consumer keep using headline-stats). This is what lets the site-selection landing place each pack as a light on a map instead of an arbitrary composition.

Everything stays sector-agnostic and mining-agnostic. The consumer will not parse a theme title for meaning, will not rank themes itself, and will not infer which solution is best — it renders the producer's order, counts and author words. Mining scripts remain outside the chatbot; this contract is only how their output arrives.

Contributor names on the evidence itself: for each entry in audit.source_versions (and in whatever the themes endpoint returns), the people credited by that source — author list, and where it exists an ORCID or an institution. The consumer's site-selection view can then show a story as the people who contributed to it rather than as a count of data sets, which is what it shows today because names are not available. Names only; no contact details.
acceptance: A pack with no /v1/themes endpoint renders the existing decision-map catalogue exactly as it does today — this request is additive and must not regress TR-VIS-0008.
A theme with two solutions from two different authors shows both, each with its own write-up and byline, and opening either yields that author's declared basemap and initial view.

A solution that declares a dark basemap renders dark, and a solution that declares none renders on the consumer default, in the same session, without a page reload and without changing the reader's global theme.
A theme mined from 40 conversations sorts above one mined from 3, using the producer's counts; the consumer never recomputes the ranking.
A theme with zero solutions renders as an open question with its mined count, and offers no solution affordance.
A solution whose validation failed keeps the TR-VIS-0008 treatment: evidence and failed checks shown, no place styled as selected, no recommendation implied — the write-up does not override this.
Write-ups render as text only: any embedded HTML or script in the markdown is inert.
capabilities.bounds (or centroid) for two packs is enough for the landing to place both without any additional query.

A pack whose sources carry author lists renders the landing's contributor view with people's names on hover; a pack whose sources carry none renders the same view with the data set titles and says so, with no placeholder names invented.
notes: The consumer is building the Themes centre now against the existing catalogue: `recipe.questions` stands in for a theme's question group, `decision` + `product` + `validation.method` stand in for the write-up, and the consumer's own basemaps are used until a presentation block exists. Every one of those is a visible placeholder, not a guess dressed as data — where the producer says nothing, the consumer shows less rather than inventing. Two consumer boundaries hold regardless of what this request delivers: an author's prose is rendered as text and never executed, and a failed validation can never be turned into a recommendation by anything an author writes. A second consumer experiment is live behind a landing toggle: each site is drawn as its contributing dots. Until author names exist, one dot is one data set and the label says 'data sets behind this story' — the shape of the view is right, the nouns are the honest ones available.
